slides.title: Arrays and Strings
slides.main: Almost everything else follows from one simple fact: an array is contiguous.

captions: The array is the brick almost everything else is built from
Where instant access by index comes from
Insertion, deletion and a growing list: what they cost
Prefix sums and difference arrays: constant-time queries
Strings: arrays again, but immutable and with Unicode

body.text: Twenty exercises at the end of the chapter: from the second maximum to the first missing positive.

slides.title: Array in memory
slides.sub: An element's address is computed, not searched for
slides.main: Address = start + index × size: reading by index takes constant time.

captions: Same-size elements lie in a row, eight bytes each
Where does element number five live?
Start plus index times size: one multiplication, one addition
Not an algorithm trick but a consequence of contiguity: constant time

frames.text: time doesn't depend on length: O(1)

slides.title: Bounds and traversal
slides.sub: Half-open intervals prevent the off-by-one error
slides.main: Write intervals as [start, end): length is the difference, no gaps at the joins.

captions: In an array of ten elements, valid indexes are 0 to 9
a[10] is an error: either a stop or someone else's memory
[start, end): length is the difference, neighbors join without gaps
Traversal is one step per element: linear time

slides.title: Insertion and deletion
slides.sub: The price of contiguity is shifting
slides.main: Insert and delete in the middle: O(n); at the end: no shifts.

captions: A B C D E — and one free cell on the right
Insert at position 2: shift right to left, starting from the last
X took the freed spot
Deletion is the mirror image: the right part shifts left and closes the gap
The further left, the more shifts: n at the start, none at the end

frames.text: removed X — everything to the left moves one step
expensive at the start, free at the end

slides.title: Dynamic array
slides.sub: Capacity and length are two different numbers
slides.main: Out of room: allocate twice as much and copy. On average O(1) per append.

captions: Two numbers are stored: capacity and length. While length is smaller, write into a free cell
Out of room: length equals capacity
Allocate a block twice as large…
…copy all the old elements, once per n appends
New appends are free again until the new capacity fills up

slides.title: Why doubling
slides.sub: Geometric growth versus a fixed step
slides.main: 1 + 2 + 4 + … + n < 2n: growing by multiplication gives amortized constant time.

captions: Growing by a fixed step: many copies, each drags everything accumulated, a square
Growing twofold: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + … up to n, total copying under 2n
With a million elements: 50 billion operations versus two million
Every production list grows by multiplication; the price is only spare memory

slides.title: A gift: friendship with the cache
slides.main: A sequential pass is the cache's best friend; jumping around memory is costly.

captions: The processor reads memory not by bytes but in 64-byte lines
Access to a[0] is a miss: the whole line travels to the fast cache
Neighboring elements are already in the cache: almost free
Reached the edge of the line: one miss, then a run of hits again
Jumping around memory: a miss at every step, with the same formal complexity

frames.text: memory is a hundred times slower than the cache

slides.title: One pass
slides.sub: The part already passed is a few numbers
slides.main: Second maximum in one pass: two variables instead of sorting.

captions: Go left to right and keep two variables: the largest and the second
9 is greater than the largest: the old largest becomes the second
7 is not above the largest, but above the second: it displaces the second
The rest change nothing. One pass, constant memory

slides.title: Reversal and shift in place
slides.sub: Three reversals instead of an auxiliary array
slides.main: Cyclic shift by k: reverse everything, then the first k and the rest.

captions: Shift right by k = 2 without an auxiliary array
Step 1: reverse the whole array with two indexes meeting in the middle
Step 2: reverse the first k elements
Step 3: reverse the rest, and we get 4 5 1 2 3

slides.title: Prefix sums
slides.main: A range sum is the difference of two ready prefixes.

captions: We must answer many times: what is the sum from l to r?
Prepare once: P[i] is the sum of the first i elements
Query from 2 to 4: take two ready numbers
Difference of two prefixes: preparation O(n), each query O(1)

slides.title: Difference array
slides.sub: The flip side of prefix sums
slides.main: Adding on a range is two edits; accumulation restores the values.

captions: Command: add 5 to all elements from l = 2 to r = 5
Store not the values but the differences of neighbors
A range changes just two numbers: +5 at the start, −5 right after the end
One pass with accumulation turns differences into values

frames.text: a[i] = a[i−1] + d[i]  — O(n) for all commands

slides.title: Matrices
slides.main: In memory a matrix is a tape: address i · w + j; rows are faster than columns.

captions: A 3 × 4 matrix: for us, a table of rows and columns
In memory it is still one tape, row after row. Address is i · w + j
Walking by rows goes through memory in order: the cache is happy
Walking by columns jumps across the whole width: the cache suffers

slides.title: Strings
slides.main: Collect pieces and join once; a character is not a byte.

captions: A string is immutable: every append creates a new one
Everything accumulated is copied: 1 + 2 + 3 + … a square
Collect pieces in a list and join once: linear
Character ≠ byte: length in characters and in bytes differ

slides.title: Techniques and summary
slides.main: An array is contiguity at the price of rigidity; practice: twenty exercises.

captions: Reading by index in constant time is the reward for contiguity
Appending at the end is amortized constant; inserting in the middle is O(n)
Prefix and difference arrays make queries constant
Strings: collect in pieces, join once
Twenty exercises, from the second maximum to the first missing
